title: Senior's toolkit: moving fast in vim
summary: The motions fast vim users actually lean on: words, find-on-line, brackets, search under the cursor and the jump list.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: moving fast in vim
steps.body: Fast vim users rarely press `j` ten times. They jump to the thing they mean: a word, a character, a bracket, a search match, the last place they were.

toolkit.what: Move by word. Lowercase stops at punctuation; uppercase (WORD) only at spaces, which is what you want for paths and URLs.
Jump to a character on the current line. The quickest way to reach an argument or a value in a long line.
Line start, first non-blank character, line end. `^` is the one you want in indented code.
Top of file, bottom of file, a line number. Paste the line number from a stack trace and you are there.
Jump to the matching bracket: `(` and `)`, `[` and `]`, `{` and `}`. Finds where a block ends, or shows that a bracket is missing.
flags: to the partner of the bracket under or after the cursor
delete up to and including the partner

toolkit.what: Search for the word under the cursor without typing it, then step through the matches. The everyday "where else is this used?".
flags: search forward / backward for the whole word

toolkit.what: Walk back and forward through the jump list: every search, `G`, `%` and file change is a jump. After a search, Ctrl+O takes you back to where you were.
flags: jump back to the last jump

toolkit.what: Centre the screen on the cursor, scroll half a page down or up. Keeps context visible while reading logs.

steps.prompt: Match each motion to where it takes you.
pairs: the first non-blank character of the line
just before the next comma on the line
the next use of the word under the cursor
back to where you were before the jump

steps.prompt: The build says `OrderService.cs(214,17): error CS1513: } expected`. You open the file. What is the fastest way to see which block is not closed?
options: `214G`, put the cursor on a `{` near there and press `%` to see where its partner is
Press `j` 213 times, then read every line
steps.explain: `214G` (or `:214`) jumps to the line from the error. `%` on each opening brace shows its partner; the one that jumps somewhere unexpected, or does not move, is the missing brace.

steps.prompt: Does the motion stay on the current line, or can it go anywhere in the file?
The cursor is on the `c` of `connect`. You press `f(` and then `%`. Type the one character that sits just to the right of the cursor.
steps.explain: `f(` lands on the first `(`, right after `connect`. `%` jumps to its partner, the last `)` on the line, and the `;` follows it. The inner brackets of `host(...)` and `port(...)` are skipped because they are balanced.

steps.prompt: You searched `/retryCount` to check its declaration 400 lines up. Now you want to go straight back to the line you were editing. What do you press?
steps.explain: The search was a jump, so `Ctrl+O` returns to where you started. `N` goes to the previous match, `u` undoes an edit, `gg` goes to the top.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Each time you catch yourself holding `j` or `l`, ask which jump would get you there: a line number, `f`, `%` or `*`. Use `Ctrl+O` freely after every search; it turns "look something up" into a round trip of two keys.
